Empirical Research Plan — “Does reducing class size improve student achievement?  Evidence from Maimonides’ rule in Israel, 1991–1992”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (FRD) implemented as two–stage least squares (2SLS).

Rationale  
• The running variable (RV) is the school-grade enrollment count.  
• The administrative rule generates sharp, discontinuous jumps in expected (predicted) class size at every multiple of 40, but the realized class size declines only imperfectly (schools can slightly deviate, principals may reshuffle).  Hence treatment assignment is discontinuous but not deterministic → fuzzy RDD.  
• FRD provides a local average treatment effect (LATE) for schools just below vs. just above each threshold.  
• Because the same RV and instrument arise from the rule, the FRD can be implemented as an IV where “predicted class size” (or the interaction of “above cutoff” with a polynomial in RV) instruments actual class size.  
• Unlike DiD or event studies, no time variation is exploited; we rely on cross-sectional discontinuities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_it  = average class size of school i in grade g in year t (continuous).

Instrument / Running variable  
RV_it = enrollment_it  (number of pupils in school i, grade g, year t).

Cutoffs  
k × 40 for k = 1,2,3,…  In practice we focus on the first two (40 and 80) where density is highest.

Treatment indicator (for FRD)  
Z_it = 1[ enrollment_it > 40 ]  (or >80 for the second threshold).  
Z_it is 0 just below and 1 just above; its interaction with a flexible function of RV serves as the excluded instrument.

Control group  
Schools with enrollment just below the cutoff (e.g., 30–40) form the counterfactual for those just above (41–50).

Timing  
Single-shot cross-sectional setting; treatment “occurs” contemporaneously with enrollment counts determining class formation in the same academic year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes  
Absent the rule, mean test scores would vary smoothly with enrollment; any discontinuity at the threshold is attributable to the class-size change.

Plausibility: Parents are rarely able to precisely choose enrollment counts at the school-grade level; Israel has residence-based school assignment and no high-stakes funding formulas at 40-pupil points. Continuity in pre-determined covariates can be empirically tested.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable  
Schools, parents, or administrators cannot perfectly target 40, 80 pupils to gain smaller classes.

Plausibility: Class formation decisions occur after enrollment is observed; individual families moving would have negligible impact on an entire grade’s count. Testable via McCrary density test.

A3. Strong first stage (relevance)  
Crossing the cutoff must cause a sizable fall in class size.

Plausibility: By construction, going from 40 to 41 splits the cohort roughly in half (≈ –20 pupils), a very large shift.  Can be verified in the data.

A4. Exclusion restriction  
The cutoff affects achievement only through class size (no other simultaneous school-level policy kicks in exactly at 41, 81, …).

Plausibility: The rule concerns only class formation.  We will verify smoothness of observable school resources, teacher qualifications, etc. across the threshold.

A5. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers across schools around the cutoff).

Plausibility: Geographic clustering of schools could create peer externalities, but these are likely minor over one-year horizons.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation Strategies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / bunching at enrollment = 40  
• McCrary test on RV density.  
• Donut RDD (drop schools with 39–41 enrollment) if manipulation suspected.  
• Show covariate balance to reinforce continuity.

T2. Compositional changes (student ability, SES) at threshold  
• Test discontinuities in predetermined covariates: percent disadvantaged, prior-year test scores (grade-3), gender share, etc.  
• Control for smooth functions of these covariates or use inverse-probability weighting.

T3. Other resource adjustments triggered by class split (e.g., hiring an extra teacher may improve quality directly, not only via smaller class size).  
• Include teacher quality proxies (average teacher experience / education) as controls and test for discontinuity.  
• Interpret estimate as “class-size bundle”; discuss in robustness section.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # fast IV / RDD estimation
library(rdrobust)     # robust RDD inference
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data (assume one row per school–grade–year)
dat <- fread("israel_classes_9192.csv")

# 2. Variable construction
dat[, rv := enrollment]                           # running variable
dat[, cutoff40 := 1 * (rv > 40)]                 # indicator for first threshold
dat[, dist40 := rv - 40]                         # centered distance
# Predicted (Maimonides) class size
dat[, pred_size := rv / (floor( (rv - 1) / 40 ) + 1) ]

# 3. Sample restriction: keep grades 4–5, cohorts 30–55 around first cutoff
sample <- dat[grade %in% c(4,5) & rv >= 30 & rv <= 55]

# 4. First-stage (check relevance)
fs <- feols(class_size ~ cutoff40 + poly(dist40,2) | 0, data = sample)
summary(fs)

# 5. 2SLS main effect (FRD)
iv_main <- feols(test_score ~ 1 | class_size ~ cutoff40 + poly(dist40,2),
                 data = sample, se = "hc3")
summary(iv_main)

# 6. Graphical validation
ggplot(sample, aes(x = dist40, y = class_size)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x,2), se = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "First stage: Class size vs. enrollment relative to cutoff")

# 7. Robustness check: rdrobust with different bandwidths
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = sample$test_score,
                   x = sample$dist40,
                   c = 0,
                   fuzzy = sample$class_size)      # fuzzy RDD
summary(rd_out)
```

Notes  
• Extend code to loop over multiple thresholds (40, 80, 120) and pool estimates.  
• Add covariate balance tests (replace `class_size` with covariate in rdrobust).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior from STAR and prior Maimonides literature: a 5-pupil reduction (≈1 SD of class size) should raise test scores by about 0.10–0.15 student-level SDs (roughly 2–3 percentiles).  Direction: negative relationship—smaller classes → higher scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  (Fuzzy RDD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. No manipulation of running variable around cutoff ………………… 1  
C2. Continuity of baseline covariates at cutoff ……………………………… 1  
C3. Strong first stage (jump in class size) ……………………………………… 1  
C4. Correct bandwidth / polynomial choice robustness ………………… 0.5 (depends on checks)  
C5. Exclusion: cutoff affects outcomes only via class size …………… 0.5 (possible teacher-quality channel)

Overall score = 4/5 → credible but demands careful robustness analysis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages the sharp institutional rule to deliver a transparent, well-identified estimate of the causal impact of class size on academic achievement.
